sword_marker_records.content_osis: <div sID="gen12966" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="124" osisID="Ps.124" sID="Ps.124"/> <div eID="gen12966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12967" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12968" type="x-p"/> David penned this psalm (we suppose) upon occasion of some great deliverance which God wrought for him and his people from some very threatening danger, which was likely to have involved them all in ruin, whether by foreign invasion, or intestine insurrection, is not certain; whatever it was he seems to have been himself much affected, and very desirous to affect others, with the goodness of God, in making a way for them to escape. To him he is careful to give all the glory, and takes none to himself as conquerors usually do. I. He here magnifies the greatness of the danger they were in, and of the ruin they were at the brink of, <reference osisRef="Ps.124.1-Ps.124.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. He gives God the glory of their escape, <reference osisRef="Ps.124.6-Ps.124.7">ver. 6, 7 compared with ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.124.1-Ps.124.2">2</reference>. III. He takes encouragement thence to trust in God, <reference osisRef="Ps.124.8">ver. 8</reference>. In singing this psalm, besides the application of it to any particular deliverance wrought for us and our people, in our days and the days of our fathers, we may have in our thoughts the great work of our redemption by Jesus Christ, by which we were rescued from the powers of darkness.

Of the malice of men, by which they were reduced to the very brink of ruin. Why <hi type="italic">their wrath was kindled against us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.124.3">v. 3</reference>); something or other they were angry at, and then no less would serve than the destruction of those they had conceived a displeasure against. <hi type="italic">Wrath is cruel and anger is outrageous.</hi> Their wrath was kindled as fire ready to consume us. How far it went, and how fatal it would have been if it had gone a little further: "We should have been devoured as a lamb by a lion, not only slain, but <hi type="italic">swallowed up,</hi> so that there would have been no relics of us remaining, swallowed up with so much haste, ere we were aware, that we should have gone down alive to the pit. We should have been deluged as the low grounds by a land-flood or the sands by a high spring-tide." This similitude he dwells upon, with the ascents which bespeak this a song of degrees, or risings, like the rest. <hi type="italic">The waters had overwhelmed us.</hi> What of us? Why <hi type="italic">the stream had gone over our souls,</hi> our lives, our comforts, all that is dear to us. What waters? Why <hi type="italic">the proud waters.</hi> God suffers the enemies of his people sometimes to prevail very far against them, that his own power may appear the more illustrious in their deliverance. <div eID="gen12971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12972" type="x-p"/> II. Of the goodness of God, by which they were rescued from the very brink of ruin: "<hi type="italic">The Lord was on our side;</hi> and, <hi type="italic">if he had not been so,</hi> we should have been undone." 1. "God was on our side; he took our part, espoused our cause, and appeared for us. He was our helper, and a very present help, a help on our side, nigh at hand.
